hints: Think about what a free-living alga in seawater might run short of, compared to living inside an animal cell that is constantly respiring.
Link that extra supply to the part of photosynthesis that uses carbon dioxide, and consider other conditions like temperature or ions that are more stable inside a host.
walkthrough:
What limits photosynthesis in the sea**
Free-living algae depend on dissolved carbon dioxide in seawater, which can be in low concentration and diffuse slowly. Inside an animal cell, you are sitting right next to mitochondria that are giving out carbon dioxide all the time.

Why the polyp helps the alga fix more carbon**
The coral polyp is an animal, so it carries out aerobic respiration and releases carbon dioxide. That carbon dioxide is the substrate for the Calvin cycle in the algal chloroplast. More substrate when other factors are not limiting means a faster light-independent rate. A stable, warmer temperature and a supply of mineral ions from the host metabolism also help keep enzymes working fast.

Final answer: Algae inside polyps receive a higher / non-limiting supply of carbon dioxide from coral polyp aerobic respiration for the Calvin cycle / light-independent reactions. Temperature / named mineral ions are also higher / more favourable, increasing rate of photosynthesis.

hints: Recall the technique that separates a mixture of coloured chloroplast pigments using their different solubilities in a solvent.
Think how you would apply a tiny concentrated spot of algal extract so it does not spread too much at the start.
Picture the chromatogram standing in solvent - where must the start line be relative to the solvent level, and what do you let happen?
Remember how you turn distances moved into a number that identifies each pigment by comparison with known values.
walkthrough:
Setting up the chromatogram**
Use paper or thin-layer chromatography. Draw a pencil baseline near the base - pencil because ink would dissolve and separate itself. Spot a small drop of concentrated algal pigment extract onto the line, let it dry, then spot again on the same place to build up a concentrated spot that stays small.

Running the separation**
Stand the paper / TLC plate upright in a suitable organic solvent, with the baseline just above the solvent level so the spot is not washed off. Different pigments are more or less soluble in the solvent and stick more or less to the paper, so the solvent travelling up by capillarity carries them at different speeds and separates them into spots.

Identifying by Rf**
When the solvent front has nearly reached the top, mark its position. Measure for each spot: distance from baseline to centre of pigment spot and distance from baseline to solvent front. Calculate $R_f = \frac{\text{distance travelled by pigment}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent front}}$. Compare each $R_f$ and colour with known $R_f$ values to identify chlorophyll a, peridinin, chlorophyll c2, dinoxanthin and beta-carotene.

Final answer: Use paper / thin-layer chromatography. Place a spot of pigment extract on a pencil baseline, dry and re-spot to concentrate. Stand in organic solvent with baseline above solvent, allow solvent to move up. Measure distance moved by each pigment and by solvent front, calculate $R_f = \frac{\text{distance travelled by pigment}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent front}}$ and compare with known $R_f$ values to identify pigments.

hints: Scan Table 2.2 and count how many of the 10 absorption peaks fall inside the lamp range of 400-490 nm.
Check Table 2.1 to see which two pigments dominate the total, and where their peaks lie.
Connect more light absorbed to faster algal photosynthesis and then to what the coral polyp gains from its symbiont.
walkthrough:
Matching lamps to absorption peaks**
Look at Table 2.2. Chlorophyll a has a 430 nm peak, peridinin 456 and 485 nm, chlorophyll c2 450 and 396 nm, dinoxanthin 442 and 471 nm, beta-carotene 454 and 480 nm. That is 8 out of 10 peaks inside 400-490 nm. In other words, violet-blue lamps hit the absorption maxima of almost every pigment very well.

Why the abundant pigments matter most**
From Table 2.1, chlorophyll a and peridinin each make up 39% of the total, together 78%. They are the main light harvesters, and both absorb strongly in violet-blue. So the lamp output is matched to the pigments the algae have most of.

From light absorption to coral growth**
More photons absorbed means more excitation of chlorophyll, more ATP and NADPH for the Calvin cycle, so a faster rate of photosynthesis. The algae pass excess sugars, amino acids and oxygen to the polyp. With more food and energy for respiration, protein synthesis and calcium carbonate skeleton formation, coral growth rate increases.

Final answer: Most pigments absorb strongly in violet-blue 400-490 nm / 8 out of 10 peaks in this range. Chlorophyll a (39%) and peridinin (39%) are most abundant and both have peaks in this range. More light absorbed increases rate of algal photosynthesis, supplying more products to coral, so coral growth increases.
